architect.message: setup() discards every error from try_setup (`Err(_)`). The old code fell back only on ENOSYS/EPERM and surfaced other errors (e.g. ENOMEM, EMFILE, memlock limits). Now those failures silently degrade to spawn_blocking with no signal to the user. The behavior is documented on enable_io_uring, but consider limiting the swallow to ENOSYS/EPERM and returning other errors from build(), or at least noting the behavior change in the PR.

lang-rust.message: UringContext::setup maps every setup error to `None` with `Err(_)`. Before this PR, check_and_init only collapsed ENOSYS and EPERM and returned other errors (ENOMEM, EMFILE, registration failures) to the fs call. Those unexpected failures now fall back to spawn_blocking with no error, log, or metric, so a misconfigured host looks identical to an unsupported kernel. The doc comment states the fallback, so this is a deliberate trade-off, but it removes the only signal a user has when io_uring silently stops being used. Consider at least keeping ENOSYS/EPERM as the quiet path and recording other errors somewhere observable.

`enable_all()` calls `enable_io_uring()` under the io-uring cfg. That now sets `enable_io_uring = true`, so every runtime built with `enable_all()` on a build with this feature eagerly creates a 256-entry io_uring ring and registers its fd with the reactor at build time, even if the runtime never performs an fs operation. Before this PR the same call only enabled the I/O driver, and the ring was created lazily. The PR description does not mention this consequence for enable_all users. Confirm this eager allocation is intended for the default builder path, or gate it separately.

`driver_with_uring_sets_up_ring` (and the other ready_handle-based tests) return early when io_uring is unavailable, so on hosts that block io_uring (seccomp, io_uring_disabled sysctl) the test passes without asserting anything. This matches the existing pattern in `register_op_keeps_entry_on_submit_failure`, so it is not a regression, but the new test adds no coverage on those hosts. Acceptable as-is because the other tests skip the same way.

pragmatist.message: Every setup error is now swallowed (`Err(_)`). Before, only ENOSYS and EPERM fell back and other errors, such as EMFILE or ENOMEM, reached the caller. Now a user who asked for io_uring and hit a resource limit gets silent blocking-pool fallback with no way to find out. The docs do state the fallback. Consider limiting the fallback to the previous ENOSYS/EPERM cases and returning other errors from `build()`, since `build()` can now fail anyway. Otherwise, say in the PR that this change is intentional.

skeptic.message: setup() discards every error with `Err(_)`. The old code fell back only for ENOSYS and EPERM and returned other errors (ENOMEM, EMFILE, a failed mio register) to the caller. Those failures are now silent. A user who opted in with enable_io_uring() gets blocking-pool fallback with no signal, and a resource problem looks the same as a kernel without io_uring. Consider falling back only for ENOSYS and EPERM and propagating the rest from build(), or at least document the choice and add a test for it.
skeptic.suggestion: Err(e) if matches!(e.raw_os_error(), Some(libc::ENOSYS | libc::EPERM)) => (Self::new(), None),

skeptic.message: io_uring was previously set up lazily for any runtime that had an IO driver. It is now set up only when enable_io_uring() was called, so runtimes built with enable_all() or enable_io() no longer use io_uring for fs operations. This looks intended, but it is a silent behavior change for tokio_unstable users and should be called out in the PR or docs. The tests also need to cover that enable_io() alone falls back to spawn_blocking.

dropped.message: setup() swallows all io_uring setup errors rather than only ENOSYS/EPERM.
enable_all() now eagerly creates an io_uring ring at build time.
driver_with_uring_sets_up_ring returns early on hosts without io_uring, so it asserts nothing there; matches existing test pattern.

findings.message: `UringContext::setup` throws away every error from `try_setup` (`Err(_) => (Self::new(), None)`). The old `check_and_init` fell back only on ENOSYS (no io_uring) and EPERM (blocked by seccomp, see #7691). Every other error, such as ENOMEM, EMFILE, memlock limits or a failed mio `register`, went back to the caller. Now those failures quietly fall back to the blocking pool. A user who called `enable_io_uring()` and hit a resource limit can't tell that from a kernel without io_uring. Nothing is returned, logged or counted. `build()` already returns `io::Result` and can fail for other reasons, so you could keep ENOSYS/EPERM as the quiet fallback and return other errors from `build()`. If swallowing everything is intended, say so in the PR and add a test for it.
findings.suggestion: Err(e) if matches!(e.raw_os_error(), Some(libc::ENOSYS | libc::EPERM)) => (Self::new(), None),

findings.message: io_uring setup now depends on the new `enable_io_uring` flag instead of happening on first use for any runtime with an IO driver. This changes behaviour in two ways that the PR doesn't mention. (1) A runtime built with only `enable_io()` no longer uses io_uring for fs operations. (2) `enable_all()` calls `enable_io_uring()` under the io-uring cfg (builder.rs:419), so every such runtime now creates a 256-entry ring and registers its fd at build time, even if it never does an fs operation. Both look intended, but they should be in the PR notes or docs. A test that `enable_io()` alone falls back to spawn_blocking would also help.
